 NYC scores 90-day extension on proposed SNAP retailer rules that put bodegas at risk 
 by 
 Ariama C. Long 
 November 19, 2026 November 18, 2026

 Shop owners and anti-hunger advocates join Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani at a press conference about SNAP-authorized retailers. City Hall. Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (Ed Reed/Mayoral Photography Office.) 
 Thousands of New Yorkers lost their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits last month after the federal government imposed new work requirements on food assistance, but in an effort to get ahead of further impact, the city negotiated a delay in enforcement of the new rules for SNAP-authorized retailers, stores, and bodegas.

 The Trump administration’s H.R.1 Bill from 2025 had mandates and work requirements that went into effect on October 1. The bill mandated that states pay at least 75% of SNAP administrative costs while the federal government pays less. In addition, work requirements for able-bodied adults without dependents aged 18 to 64, and families with children aged 14 and older, are no longer eligible for an exemption. 
 One of the consequences SNAP changes and cuts have on the local economy is the loss of revenue for SNAP-authorized retailers, like mom-and-pop grocery stores, corner stores, and bodegas, and farmer’s markets that accept EBT cards. There are more than 10,000 bodegas and corner stores in the Five Boroughs, according to an analysis by the Department of City Planning. 
 Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani announces that, following negotiations with Trump administration, U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) will delay start of enforcement of new rule requiring SNAP-authorized retailers to meet expanded stocking standards. City Hall. Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (Ed Reed/Mayoral Photography Office.) 
 “Many New Yorkers use their SNAP benefits at the bodegas that line our streets and sit at the corners of our intersections — the beating hearts of so many of our neighborhoods,” said Mamdani at a November 13 press conference . “On September 4, the USDA said that if small businesses did not meet these new standards by November 4, they would lose their ability to accept SNAP.”
 On November 2, Mamdani’s team sent a letter to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The mayor said after negotiations with the Trump administration, the USDA agreed to a 90-day extension for a new rule requiring SNAP-authorized retailers to meet expanded stocking standards for dairy, grains, proteins, and fruits and vegetables. 
 The stock rule was supposed to go into effect on November 4, but the city said the implementation guidance was not issued until September 4. Without enough time, neighborhood stores and bodegas risked losing their ability to accept SNAP and a significant share of their sales. Stores removed from the program would also have to wait six months before reapplying. 
 “We recognize that more time is not enough on its own. Small businesses are still facing significant challenges and will require support,” said Mamdani.
 SNAP purchases generally make up 15% to 20% of a bodega’s revenue, depending on the number of recipients in the neighborhood. In the Bronx, SNAP revenue among bodega owners can be as high as 30%, he said.
 “In many Bronx neighborhoods, the local bodega is one of the most accessible places to buy groceries, for our seniors, working parents, and residents who depend on SNAP benefits,” said City Councilmember Amanda Farías, who chairs the Committee on Women and Gender Equity and co-chairs the Bronx Delegation, in a statement. “We cannot expect small business owners to navigate these new federal requirements without adequate time and guidance, especially when their ability to accept SNAP seriously impacts whether families can continue shopping close to home.”
 City Councilmember Alexa Avilés added that families often depend on bodegas to get food, even when they didn’t have money to pay for it. 
 “My family depended very much on the generosity of the bodegas to give us food and to hope that one day, we were going to pay them back,” she said at the press conference, “and that’s the contract that we are talking about that is so important in communities.”
 Mamdani and the city’s Mom and Pop Czar Delia Awusi said more than 100 bodega owners reached out to the city with concerns and to request more time. They held a roundtable discussion with bodega owners at City Hall on October 29.
 “This 90-day extension gives us time to better understand the new requirement and regulation, and prepare our changes to continue our business,” said United Bodegas of America (UBA) President Radhames Rodriguez. “Nuestras bodegas. Nuestras bodegas le servimos a la comunidad. Nosotros somos la comunidad.”
 Federal SNAP changes also led to about 30,000 New Yorkers losing benefits last month, according to the city. The city began outreach efforts to re-enroll as many people as possible and assist more than 220,000 New Yorkers who were at risk of losing SNAP benefits. More than 98% of eligible SNAP recipients have maintained access to food assistance, said the city.
